title: Fowler Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fowler wells have a 35-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $7,200-$13,900.
h1: Fowler, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Fowler sits on the plains, where permitted wells are generally shallow compared with many Colorado mountain and foothill areas. In the records within 5 miles of town, the median well depth is 35 feet, and the middle half runs from 28 to 45 feet. That does not make every lot predictable: the deepest recorded well reaches 1,520 feet, and the local records include both alluvial and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers.

This page uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records to explain what nearby wells produce, how the water level has changed in the records, what drilling may cost, and which questions deserve attention before buying land or starting construction.

sections.heading: Fowler wells are usually shallow, but the outliers matter
sections.html:
The typical Fowler well is shallow. The median recorded depth is 35 feet, while the middle half falls between 28 and 45 feet. Ninety-seven percent of wells are under 100 feet, so a driller bidding a normal residential well will likely be working in that range rather than planning a several-hundred-foot hole.

There are exceptions. Two percent of the wells fall between 100 and 300 feet, and one percent are deeper than 600 feet; the deepest record is 1,520 feet. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while a smaller number identify Alluvial or Quaternary Alluvium. A nearby well is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee for a new borehole.

sections.heading: Recorded Fowler yields are strong, with limited reporting
sections.html:
Yield records look favorable, but only 64 wells report a pump yield. Among those records, the median is 290.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 712.5 gallons per minute. Eighty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 19% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 2% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures should not be treated as a promise for an untested lot. A reported pumping rate may reflect a particular test and well construction. Ask for the well-construction report and pumping information for nearby parcels, and have the driller explain what rate is appropriate for the intended household, stock, or irrigation use.

sections.heading: Fowler’s water levels deserve a closer look
sections.html:
Among the 23 wells that report a static water level, the median depth to water is 20 feet, with the middle half between 12 and 24 feet below the surface. That is consistent with the shallow well depths common around Fowler, but static water level is not the same as the water available while pumping.

The decade comparison shows a deeper median measured water level in the more recent records: 16 feet below surface in the 2010s and 23 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water levels may be lower in the newer measurements, but the sample is small and the wells, locations, and measurement conditions may differ. A buyer should obtain a current level and pumping test rather than assume the decade pattern applies to every property.

sections.heading: Fowler’s permit history shows long-term drilling activity
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records list 671 permitted wells within the study area, with 481 recorded as constructed. Of those, 479 report a total depth, 64 report a pump yield, and 23 report a static water level. Permits span the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025, so the database reflects both older rural development and recent construction.

The busiest named drillers in these records are Crandall, H A, with 51 wells; Broce Drilling, identified as Broce, Frank R., with 35; and Hoffman, identified as Hoffman, Earl, with 19. These names show who appears most often in the records, not who is available or necessarily best for a current job. Verify licensing, insurance, references, and the proposed casing, grout, pump, and testing scope before signing a contract.

sections.heading: What a new Fowler well may cost
sections.html:
For Fowler’s alluvium and plains sedimentary ground, the drilling rate model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 35 feet, the drilled hole alone models to about $1,200 to $1,900. That is only the borehole portion of the job and should not be confused with a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,200 to $13,900 at the median depth. A quote can move outside that range because of access, casing and grout requirements, pump size, water treatment, longer utility runs, difficult ground, or an unexpectedly deep hole. Get the driller to separate drilling, completion, testing, and site work so bids can be compared accurately.

sections.heading: Checks to make before buying or building near Fowler
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main warning in the reported Fowler data, but incomplete reporting means a dry hole or poor-producing location remains possible. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable even where nearby records look good. Confirm the permit status and allowed use with DWR; an exempt household-use well is subject to its permit terms, including the 35 gallons-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit. Irrigation or other uses may require different authorization, and an augmentation plan can matter in an over-appropriated basin.

Environmental screening also matters. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, with 0 historic mine features. Test the water for local concerns and ordinary household contaminants. Before building, confirm septic setbacks, soil conditions, drainage, access for a rig, and separation between the well, septic system, and proposed house.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Fowler lot
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring well records, but do not stop there. Compare depths, aquifer descriptions, reported yields, water levels, use types, and construction dates on parcels closest to the lot. Then have a Colorado-licensed driller review the location, access, geology, intended use, and permit path before you rely on a purchase budget.

For a home, make the contract contingent on acceptable well documentation, water quality, and a pumping test when feasible. Budget separately for the well, pump system, electrical work, trenching, septic, and site access. If the property is intended for irrigation, stock, or more than ordinary household use, confirm the legal water supply before closing rather than assuming a shallow, high-yield neighboring well establishes your rights.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fowler, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Fowler is 35 feet, and the middle half ranges from 28 to 45 feet. Ninety-seven percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet. The range is not uniform, however: the deepest record is 1,520 feet, so nearby well records and a driller’s site review still matter for a specific parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fowler?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,200 to $1,900. A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $7,200 to $13,900. Access, depth, equipment, casing, grout, and utility distance can change the final quote.

faq.q: How much water do Fowler wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 64 Fowler-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 290.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 712.5 gallons per minute, and 80% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Because yield data are limited, a buyer should request a pumping test rather than rely only on the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Fowler, Colorado?
faq.a: Well safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The mapped area includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, so location-specific testing is important. Test a proposed home well through a qualified laboratory and review the result with a water professional before drinking it or choosing treatment.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Fowler, Colorado?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 16 feet below surface in the 2010s and 23 feet in the 2020s. That newer measurement is deeper, which may indicate lower water levels, but only 23 wells report static water levels and the measurements may not be comparable. A current level and pumping test are better evidence for one property.
